agenthubSkills.name: filesystem
agenthubSkills.description: Use for file discovery and edits in the consuming SolidX project (solid-ui and solid-api) with the filesystem tool.
agenthubSkills.body:
# Filesystem Use this skill for deterministic file discovery and edits in the consuming SolidX project: frontend code in `solid-ui/**` and backend code in `solid-api/**`. ## Tool Boundary - Use `filesystem` as the primary mechanism for file discovery, inspection, editing, and creation. - Do not fall back to shell commands for file lookup or reads when `filesystem(action: "search"|"read")` can provide the context. - Do not use shell commands to create or edit files. - Use `bash` only for verification work that `filesystem` cannot do, such as builds, typechecks, or test runs. ## Path and Root Rules - Paths are relative to the consuming project root (`CONTAINER_SOLIDX_CONSUMING_PROJECT_ROOT`, or `SOLIDX_PROJECT_ROOT`). Absolute paths must stay under that root. - Frontend code lives under `solid-ui/**`, backend code under `solid-api/**`. - `path_outside_workspace` means the target resolved outside the root; use a project-relative path. ## Reading SolidX Metadata SolidX modules, models, fields, views, menus, roles, and the rest are defined in metadata JSON files inside `solid-api`. Read them with `filesystem`; never guess module, model, or field names. ### Where metadata lives | Source | Path | | --- | --- | | A project module | `solid-api/src//metadata/-metadata.json` | | SolidX core (read-only) | `solid-api/node_modules/@solidxai/core/src/seeders/seed-data/solid-core-metadata.json` (or `.../dist/seeders/seed-data/...` when `src` is absent) | | Email / SMS template bodies | `solid-api/src//metadata/email-templates/*.handlebars.html`, `.../sms-templates/*.handlebars.txt` | Never edit the core metadata file; it is a package dependency. ### File shape Top-level keys of a metadata file: - `moduleMetadata`: the module (`name`, `displayName`, ...) and `moduleMetadata.models[]`. Each model has `singularName`, `pluralName`, `displayName`, `tableName`, `dataSource`, `userKeyFieldUserKey`, and `fields[]`. - Each field has `name`, `displayName`, `type` (`shortText`, `longText`, `int`, `boolean`, `date`, `selectionStatic`, `relation`, `computed`, ...), `ormType`, `required`, `unique`, `defaultValue`, and type-specific keys such as `selectionStaticValues` (`"value:Label"` strings) or `relationType` / `relationCoModelSingularName`. - `views[]` (`name`, `type` list/form/kanban/card/tree, `modelUserKey`, `layout`), `actions[]`, `menus[]`, `roles[]`, `permissions[]`, `securityRules[]`, `listOfValues[]`, `scheduledJobs[]`, `emailTemplates[]`, `smsTemplates[]`, `modelSequences[]`, `savedFilters[]`, `dashboards[]`, `mediaStorageProviders[]`. Columns in the database use snake_case of the field `name` (for example `lastLoadError` is `last_load_error`) unless the field sets `columnName`. ### How to read it Metadata files are large; locate first, then read narrow line windows. 1. List the modules: ```json { "action": "search", "query": "\"moduleMetadata\"", "path": "solid-api/src", "glob": "*-metadata.json", "context_lines": 0 } ``` Each match is one module's metadata file; its folder under `solid-api/src` is the module name. 2. Find a model by name: ```json { "action": "search", "query": "\"singularName\": \"order\"", "path": "solid-api/src", "glob": "*-metadata.json", "context_lines": 0 } ``` The match gives the file and line number where the model definition starts. 3. Read the model and its fields from that line, in windows: ```json { "action": "read", "path": "solid-api/src/sales/metadata/sales-metadata.json", "start_line": 120, "end_line": 420 } ``` Keep reading the next window until the model's `fields` array closes. 4. Find views, menus, or roles for a model with a targeted search, for example `"modelUserKey": "order"` or `"name": "order-list-view"`, then read around the match. 5. For core models (users, roles, settings, agent registries), search and read the core metadata file by passing its full path as `path`; it is outside `solid-api/src`, so searches of that folder never reach it. Use the metadata you read to build correct API calls, SQL (`run_read_only_postgres` or `run_read_only_mssql`), and code edits. When a field is a relation, read the co-model's definition as well. ## Tool Contract `filesystem` exposes four actions. ### `filesystem(action: "search")` Use to locate symbols and usages before edits. - `query`: string, required. A regex/text pattern, not plain literal text. If you copy source code into it, escape regex metacharacters first (`{ } ( ) [ ] . * + ? | ^ $ \`). For multiple literal snippets, escape each and join them with `|`. - `path`: string, optional. Defaults to `solid-ui`; use `solid-api` for backend. - `glob`: string, optional (for example `"*.tsx"` or `"*.ts"`). - `case_sensitive`: boolean, default `false`. - `max_matches`: integer, default `200`. - `context_lines`: integer, default `2`. ```json { "action": "search", "query": "class .*Service|@Controller|@Injectable", "path": "solid-api", "glob": "*.ts" } ``` Uses ripgrep (respects `.gitignore`, skips hidden and binary files); falls back to grep when ripgrep is unavailable. ### `filesystem(action: "read")` Use for precise inspection before editing. - `path`: string, required. - `start_line`, `end_line`: optional 1-based integers (inclusive). To read the whole file, omit them; do not send empty strings or placeholders. - `max_chars`: integer, default `20000`. `truncated: true` means read a narrower window. ```json { "action": "read", "path": "solid-ui/src/pages/orders/order-list.tsx", "start_line": 1, "end_line": 220 } ``` ### `filesystem(action: "edit")` Use for surgical changes to **existing** files. Each entry replaces `oldText` with `newText`; there are no line numbers or diffs. The applier tries an exact substring match first (first occurrence only), then a whitespace-tolerant line-by-line match. Required pre-edit discipline: - Read the target with `filesystem(action: "read")` immediately before every edit. Read enough surrounding context to make each `oldText` unique. - Build `oldText` from the returned source verbatim. Never reconstruct it from memory, an earlier version, or a partial prompt snippet. - If the file changed after the read, read it again and rebuild the edit. Do not retry a stale payload. - `path`: string, required; the file must exist. - `edits`: non-empty array of `{ "oldText": string, "newText": string }`. - `dry_run`: boolean, optional; validate without persisting. ```json { "action": "edit", "path": "solid-api/src/orders/orders.service.ts", "edits": [{ "oldText": "const enabled = false;", "newText": "const enabled = true;" }] } ``` Multiple edits apply sequentially; each sees the previous edit's result. Include 1–3 surrounding lines when needed to make `oldText` unique. Edits are atomic: if any edit fails to match, the file is unchanged. ### `filesystem(action: "write")` Use to create new files or intentionally replace a whole file. Writes are atomic (temp file + rename) and parent directories are created automatically. - `path`: string, required. - `content`: string, required; full UTF-8 content. - `overwrite`: boolean, default `false`. Without it, writing an existing file fails with `file_exists`. ```json { "action": "write", "path": "solid-ui/src/pages/landing/Landing.tsx", "content": "import React from 'react';\n\nexport function Landing() {\n return
Welcome
;\n}\n" } ``` Prefer `action: "edit"` for partial changes; reserve `overwrite: true` for genuine full rewrites. ## Recommended Flow 1. `search` to locate files and references. 2. `read` targeted line windows around the matches. 3. `edit` for surgical changes, or `write` for new files. 4. `read` the file again to confirm the change persisted before chaining dependent edits. 5. If verification is required, run build, typecheck, or test commands with `bash` after all edits. ## Conventions - For UI under `solid-ui/**`, prefer Radix UI + shadcn/ui patterns for behaviour and Tailwind CSS utilities for layout and spacing; reuse existing primitives before adding custom CSS. - For backend code, keep controller, service, and repository signatures aligned (method names, arguments, return types). - Prefer small focused edits over full-file rewrites. ## Error Repair Playbook - `search_backend_not_found`: neither ripgrep nor grep is installed; report it. - `path_not_found` (search): the `path` does not exist. Drop it (or pass an existing parent) and narrow with `glob`, e.g. `glob: "**/CurrencyExchange/*.tsx"`. Do not retry the same call. - `path_outside_workspace`: use a path relative to the project root. - `edit_no_match`: `oldText` was not found. Re-read the file and build a new `oldText` from the current content. Do not retry the same payload. - `noop_edit`: `oldText` equals `newText`; drop that entry. - `file_not_found` (edit): the file does not exist; create it with `action: "write"`. - `file_exists` (write): the file exists and `overwrite` was not set. Use `action: "edit"`, or `overwrite: true` for an intentional full rewrite. - `binary_or_non_utf8`: the file is not UTF-8 text; this tool cannot read or edit it. - Validation errors: the payload was rejected before any I/O; fix the argument types and resubmit.

agenthubSkills.description: Research a question on the web with web_search and cite sources.
agenthubSkills.body:
# Web research

Use this when the answer depends on current or external information.

1. Call `web_search` with a focused query. Start with `max_results` 5 and `fetch_pages` 0 to scan titles and snippets.
2. Pick the most authoritative results (official docs, vendor sites, standards bodies) and call `web_search` again with `fetch_pages` 2-3 to read the page text.
3. If results are thin, rephrase: add a product name, a version, or a site name; remove filler words.
4. Cross-check facts that matter against at least two independent sources.
5. Answer with the facts you verified and list the source URLs you relied on. Say clearly when sources disagree or nothing reliable was found.

Do not invent URLs or quote text you did not fetch. If `web_search` returns `search_unavailable`, wait and retry once, then tell the user.

agenthubSkills.name: postgres_query_assistant
agenthubSkills.description: Use to fetch records, explore schema, read sample data, or write SQL for user-run changes on a PostgreSQL project database with run_read_only_postgres.
agenthubSkills.body:
# PostgreSQL Query Assistant

Use this skill to query a PostgreSQL project database with `run_read_only_postgres`:
- fetch records with read-only SQL
- generate SQL for mutations the user runs themselves
- **discover schema structure** — tables, columns, types, constraints, indexes, views
- **read sample data** to understand domain objects and their attribute semantics

Before writing SQL, confirm the project database is PostgreSQL: use `filesystem(action: "search", query: "@SolidDatabaseModule", path: "solid-api/src")` to find the datasource module, `filesystem(action: "read", ...)` it, and check its `type()`. Reuse the answer for the rest of the conversation; never ask the user. If the type is `mssql`, use the `mssql_query_assistant` skill and `run_read_only_mssql` instead. A tool error `unsupported_database` means the same thing.

---

## Workflow

1. For record retrieval, build one read-only query and run it with `run_read_only_postgres`.
2. Return the rows clearly, including the filters used.
3. For mutating requests (`DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, `ALTER`, ...), optionally run supporting read-only queries with `run_read_only_postgres` to validate tables, columns, and matching rows, then write the SQL for the user without executing it.
4. Ask the user to review and run mutating SQL manually, preferably after a backup.
5. For schema or domain questions, run the discovery queries and sample reads below before drawing conclusions.

---

## PostgreSQL Rules for the Tool

- One `SELECT`, `WITH`, `EXPLAIN`, or `SHOW` statement per call; no `;`-separated statements.
- Pass values as literals in the query; quote identifiers that are reserved words or mixed case with double quotes (`"order"`).
- Limit rows with `LIMIT n` (and `OFFSET n` for paging).
- Queries run in a read-only transaction with a 30 second statement timeout.

---

## Schema Discovery

Application tables live in the `public` schema unless the project says otherwise.

Tables:
```sql
SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_type = 'BASE TABLE' ORDER BY table_name
```

Columns of a table:
```sql
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable, column_default FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name = 'orders' ORDER BY ordinal_position
```

Foreign keys (outbound from a table; swap the filter to `ccu.table_name` for inbound):
```sql
SELECT tc.table_name, kcu.column_name, ccu.table_name AS references_table, ccu.column_name AS references_column
FROM information_schema.table_constraints tc
JOIN information_schema.key_column_usage kcu ON tc.constraint_name = kcu.constraint_name AND tc.table_schema = kcu.table_schema
JOIN information_schema.constraint_column_usage ccu ON tc.constraint_name = ccu.constraint_name AND tc.table_schema = ccu.table_schema
WHERE tc.constraint_type = 'FOREIGN KEY' AND tc.table_name = 'orders'
```

Primary and unique keys: the same join filtered on `tc.constraint_type IN ('PRIMARY KEY', 'UNIQUE')`.

Indexes:
```sql
SELECT indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE schemaname = 'public' AND tablename = 'orders'
```

Views:
```sql
SELECT table_name, view_definition FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = 'public'
```

---

## Sample Data Reading

Use small, representative samples to understand domain semantics — what the data actually means, how fields are used, and what values are common. `run_read_only_postgres` always caps returned rows at `limit`, so a row-limiting clause isn't required for correctness, but a `LIMIT` is still good practice on large tables because it stops the database producing rows that would be discarded.

- **Representative sample:** fetch 10–20 rows from a table to see its shape and real values.
- **Value distribution:** `COUNT(*)` grouped by a status/type/stage column to see which business states exist and how populated each is.
- **Sparsity:** compare `COUNT(*)` with `COUNT(<column>)` to see how consistently a column is filled.
- **Relation sample:** join a parent and child table on the FK column and read a few rows to see how the relationship is used.

---

## Semantic Discovery Strategy

When the goal is to understand the domain (not just fetch specific records):

1. List all tables to get the full surface area.
2. Inspect columns and types for the tables of interest.
3. Map the relationship graph with the foreign key query.
4. Read a small sample from each key table.
5. Check value distributions for status/type/enum columns.
6. Join related tables to see how parent-child and many-to-many relationships are populated.

Only draw conclusions about domain semantics after reading actual data — column names alone are often insufficient.

---

## Rules

- `run_read_only_postgres` is strictly read-only and rejects mutating statements.
- Never attempt to execute `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER`, or other write/DDL operations.
- When the user asks to run destructive SQL, provide the exact PostgreSQL SQL and a short safety note for manual execution.
- Prefer scoped filters and a `LIMIT` for retrieval queries unless the user explicitly asks for full output.
- If table or column names are ambiguous, run the schema discovery queries first rather than guessing.
- SolidX system tables use the `ss_` prefix; leave them out of domain analysis unless the user asks about SolidX itself.

agenthubSkills.body:
# SQL Server Query Assistant

Use this skill to query a Microsoft SQL Server project database with `run_read_only_mssql`:
- fetch records with read-only T-SQL
- generate T-SQL for mutations the user runs themselves
- **discover schema structure** — tables, columns, types, constraints, indexes, views
- **read sample data** to understand domain objects and their attribute semantics

Before writing SQL, confirm the project database is SQL Server (`mssql`): use `filesystem(action: "search", query: "@SolidDatabaseModule", path: "solid-api/src")` to find the datasource module, `filesystem(action: "read", ...)` it, and check its `type()`. Reuse the answer for the rest of the conversation; never ask the user. If the type is `postgres`, use the `postgres_query_assistant` skill and `run_read_only_postgres` instead. A tool error `unsupported_database` means the same thing.

---

## Workflow

1. For record retrieval, build one read-only query and run it with `run_read_only_mssql`.
2. Return the rows clearly, including the filters used.
3. For mutating requests (`DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, `ALTER`, ...), optionally run supporting read-only queries with `run_read_only_mssql` to validate tables, columns, and matching rows, then write the SQL for the user without executing it.
4. Ask the user to review and run mutating SQL manually, preferably after a backup.
5. For schema or domain questions, run the discovery queries and sample reads below before drawing conclusions.

---

## T-SQL Rules for the Tool

- One `SELECT` or `WITH` statement per call. T-SQL runs consecutive statements even without `;`, so the tool rejects any extra statement keyword.
- Rejected: `SELECT ... INTO`, `EXEC` / `EXECUTE`, stored procedures (`sp_*`, `xp_*`), `OPENROWSET` / `OPENQUERY`, `DECLARE`, `SET`, `USE`, `WAITFOR`, and all DML/DDL.
- Limit rows with `SELECT TOP (n) ...`. There is no `LIMIT`; paging uses `ORDER BY ... OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY` and requires `ORDER BY`.
- Quote reserved or unusual identifiers with brackets (`[order]`); Unicode string literals use `N'...'`.
- Tables usually live in the `dbo` schema; qualify names as `dbo.orders` when in doubt.
- Each query has a 30 second timeout and runs in a transaction that is always rolled back.

---

## Schema Discovery

Tables:
```sql
SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES
WHERE TABLE_TYPE = 'BASE TABLE' ORDER BY TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME
```

Columns of a table:
```sql
SELECT COLUMN_NAME, DATA_TYPE, CHARACTER_MAXIMUM_LENGTH, IS_NULLABLE, COLUMN_DEFAULT
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'dbo' AND TABLE_NAME = 'orders' ORDER BY ORDINAL_POSITION
```

Foreign keys (outbound from a table; filter on `fkc.referenced_object_id` for inbound):
```sql
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(fkc.parent_object_id) AS table_name, pc.name AS column_name,
       OBJECT_NAME(fkc.referenced_object_id) AS references_table, rc.name AS references_column
FROM sys.foreign_key_columns fkc
JOIN sys.columns pc ON pc.object_id = fkc.parent_object_id AND pc.column_id = fkc.parent_column_id
JOIN sys.columns rc ON rc.object_id = fkc.referenced_object_id AND rc.column_id = fkc.referenced_column_id
WHERE fkc.parent_object_id = OBJECT_ID('dbo.orders')
```

Primary and unique keys:
```sql
SELECT tc.CONSTRAINT_TYPE, kcu.COLUMN_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLE_CONSTRAINTS tc
JOIN INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEY_COLUMN_USAGE kcu ON tc.CONSTRAINT_NAME = kcu.CONSTRAINT_NAME
WHERE tc.TABLE_NAME = 'orders' AND tc.CONSTRAINT_TYPE IN ('PRIMARY KEY', 'UNIQUE')
```

Indexes:
```sql
SELECT i.name AS index_name, i.type_desc, i.is_unique, c.name AS column_name
FROM sys.indexes i
JOIN sys.index_columns ic ON ic.object_id = i.object_id AND ic.index_id = i.index_id
JOIN sys.columns c ON c.object_id = ic.object_id AND c.column_id = ic.column_id
WHERE i.object_id = OBJECT_ID('dbo.orders') ORDER BY i.name, ic.key_ordinal
```

Views:
```sql
SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME, VIEW_DEFINITION FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS
```

---

## Sample Data Reading

Use small, representative samples to understand domain semantics — what the data actually means, how fields are used, and what values are common. `run_read_only_mssql` always caps returned rows at `limit`, so a row-limiting clause isn't required for correctness, but `TOP (n)` is still good practice on large tables because it stops the database producing rows that would be discarded.

- **Representative sample:** fetch 10–20 rows from a table to see its shape and real values.
- **Value distribution:** `COUNT(*)` grouped by a status/type/stage column to see which business states exist and how populated each is.
- **Sparsity:** compare `COUNT(*)` with `COUNT(<column>)` to see how consistently a column is filled.
- **Relation sample:** join a parent and child table on the FK column and read a few rows to see how the relationship is used.

---

## Semantic Discovery Strategy

When the goal is to understand the domain (not just fetch specific records):

1. List all tables to get the full surface area.
2. Inspect columns and types for the tables of interest.
3. Map the relationship graph with the foreign key query.
4. Read a small sample from each key table.
5. Check value distributions for status/type/enum columns.
6. Join related tables to see how parent-child and many-to-many relationships are populated.

Only draw conclusions about domain semantics after reading actual data — column names alone are often insufficient.

---

## Rules

- `run_read_only_mssql` is strictly read-only and rejects mutating statements.
- Never attempt to execute `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER`, or other write/DDL operations.
- When the user asks to run destructive SQL, provide the exact T-SQL SQL and a short safety note for manual execution.
- Prefer scoped filters and `TOP (n)` for retrieval queries unless the user explicitly asks for full output.
- If table or column names are ambiguous, run the schema discovery queries first rather than guessing.
- SolidX system tables use the `ss_` prefix; leave them out of domain analysis unless the user asks about SolidX itself.

agenthubSkills.body:
# Quality Checks

Use this skill when code changes need validation.

## Common Commands

Run each with `bash`, one command per call. Commands run in the consuming project root; set `cwd` for a sub-project instead of using `cd`.

| Check | `command` | `cwd` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backend typecheck | `npx tsc --noEmit` | `solid-api` |
| Backend tests | `npm test` | `solid-api` |
| Backend lint | `npx eslint src/ --ext .ts,.tsx` | `solid-api` |
| Frontend typecheck | `npx tsc --noEmit` | `solid-ui` |
| Frontend tests | `npm test` | `solid-ui` |

Shell operators (`&&`, `|`, `;`, redirects) are rejected.

## Rules

- Run validation after backend or frontend code edits.
- Prefer a fast typecheck or targeted test first, then broader validation if needed.
- Fix validation failures before moving on.
- A non-zero `status` means the check failed; read the end of `stdout`/`stderr` for the errors.

agenthubSkills.name: solidctl
agenthubSkills.description: Use to run SolidX CLI operations (build, seed, generate, info, test, upgrade) with bash and read their results.
agenthubSkills.body:
# Solidctl Operations

Use this skill when the user asks for SolidX CLI actions (build, seed, generate, info, test, upgrade) or a workflow needs a solidctl step after code or metadata changes.

## How to run

Run solidctl with `bash`, one command per call, from the project root (`cwd` `.`, the default):

```json
{ "command": "npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest build", "cwd": "." }
```

- Always use `npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest <command>` so no install prompt blocks the run.
- Shell operators (`&&`, `|`, `;`, redirects) are rejected; run dependent steps as separate calls and check each result before the next.
- Builds and seeds can take minutes. If the call times out, tell the user rather than re-running blindly.

## Supported Commands

- `build` - Build project artifacts (supports `--ui-only`)
- `seed` - Seed metadata/platform data (supports `--modules-to-seed <A,B>` and `--prune`)
- `info` - Inspect project information (supports `--detailed`)
- `generate` - Metadata-driven code generation (`module`, `model -n <modelName>`)
- `test` - Testing workflows (`test data --setup|--load|--teardown`, `test run ...`)
- `upgrade` - Upgrade SolidX dependencies (`--stable`, `--tag <tag>`, `--dry-run`)
- `create-app` - Scaffold a new SolidX project; not for use inside an existing project
- `release`, `legacy-migrate`, `local-upgrade`, `mcp`, `agent` - advanced/internal; do not run unless the user asks explicitly

## Practical Workflow

1. Metadata change: edit metadata (see the `filesystem` skill) -> `generate module` -> `build` -> `seed`
2. Testing: `test data --setup` -> `test data --load` -> `test run ...`
3. Upgrade: `upgrade` -> `build` -> `seed` (if metadata/platform changes are involved)

## High-Value Examples

```text
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest info --detailed
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest build
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest build --ui-only
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest generate module
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest generate model -n feeReceipt
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest seed --modules-to-seed Fees,Onboarding --prune
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest test data --setup
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest test run --module Fees --include-tags smoke
npx --yes @solidxai/solidctl@latest upgrade --stable
```

## Reading the result

`bash` returns `status`, `stdout` (tail), and `stderr` (tail).

- `status` non-zero: the command failed. Read the end of `stdout`/`stderr`, fix the cause, and retry with a corrected command.
- `status` 0 is not always success. solidctl can swallow a subprocess failure and still print a "completed" message. Treat the run as failed when `stderr` contains any of:
  - a line starting with `Error:`
  - `spawn <binary> ENOENT` (a binary solidctl calls, such as `schematics`, is not installed)
  - `UnhandledPromiseRejection`
  - `command not found` or `is not recognized as`
- Stale build: `stderr` shows `Cannot find module '...'`, `Cannot find module '....module'`, or `Path "src/..." does not exist` right after creating or changing a module. The compiled `solid-api/dist` is older than the TypeScript sources. Run `build` first, then retry the original command. Do not rewrite code for this.
- Logged-and-caught messages such as `console.error("Failed to load X:", err)` during seeding are not fatal on their own.

## Rules

- Run solidctl only for explicit CLI intent or a workflow-required step.
- Prefer a single precise command over chained speculative commands.
- If the user says `rebuild`, run `build`.
- After metadata or model changes, prefer `generate module` unless the user asks for model-only scope.
- After dependency upgrades, run `build` before further validation.
- `seed --prune`, `test data --teardown`, and `upgrade` change project data or dependencies; run them only when the user's intent is clear.
